lesson.title: Galileo Acceleration Lab
lesson.buzzAssessmentTitle: Unit 1 Lesson 3: Galileo Acceleration Lab Analysis

assessmentSettings.feedbackPolicy: Show concise process feedback after submission. Use this metadata and the Essay a. lines for BusyBee grading.

requiredUploads: Completed Galileo data chart image or screenshot

humanReviewTriggers: Student response conflicts with the uploaded chart evidence.
Student gives a partially correct explanation that does not fit the rubric cleanly.
Student describes a different but plausible measurement error.
Student answer is too vague to verify against the completed chart.
The evidence upload is missing, unreadable, or does not show all table columns.

questions.objective: Interpret interval distance as evidence of increasing speed.
questions.prompt: Describe the trend in the interval distance column. What does that trend tell you about the object's speed?
questions.requiredEvidence: Student should refer to increasing interval distances over equal time intervals.

criteria: States that interval distances increase.
Mentions equal time intervals.
Connects larger interval distances to increasing speed.
Identifies the increasing trend without explaining speed.
Explains speed increase but gives weak evidence.
Uses the right idea with imprecise wording.
Claims constant speed.
Discusses the wrong column.
Gives no usable data-based explanation.

commonMisconceptions: More total distance alone proves acceleration.
The object moves at constant speed because time intervals are equal.

feedback.partialCredit: Add how the changing interval distances show the object covers more distance during each equal time interval.
feedback.noCredit: Return to the interval distance column and compare each row to the previous one.

questions.objective: Use data evidence to identify acceleration.
questions.prompt: Explain how you can tell from the data that the object was accelerating during the fall.
questions.requiredEvidence: Student should connect acceleration to changing velocity and use increasing interval distances as evidence.

criteria: Defines or implies acceleration as changing velocity.
Uses increasing interval distances or speed over equal time intervals.
Connects the evidence to falling motion.
Says the object speeds up but gives little table evidence.
Mentions data but does not clearly state acceleration means changing velocity.
Confuses acceleration with total distance only.
Claims speed stayed the same.
Does not use data evidence.

commonMisconceptions: Acceleration means moving far, not changing velocity.
Acceleration requires a visible force arrow.

feedback.partialCredit: Add a sentence connecting the increasing interval distances to changing velocity.
feedback.noCredit: Acceleration is about velocity changing. Use the equal-time interval data to support that claim.

questions.objective: Recognize the odd-number interval ratio pattern for constant acceleration.
questions.prompt: Compare your interval ratio column to Galileo's odd-number pattern: 1, 3, 5, 7, and so on.
questions.requiredEvidence: Student should compare interval ratios to odd numbers and connect that to constant acceleration.

criteria: Identifies that interval ratios are close to odd numbers.
Explains that the odd-number pattern supports constant acceleration.
Mentions the odd-number pattern with little explanation.
Notices approximate agreement without naming the pattern clearly.
Uses the wrong pattern.
Claims ratios should all be equal.
Gives no pattern-based answer.

commonMisconceptions: The square pattern applies to interval distances instead of total distances.

feedback.partialCredit: Name the odd-number pattern and explain why it matters for constant acceleration.
feedback.noCredit: Compare the interval ratio values to 1, 3, 5, 7, and so on.

questions.objective: Recognize the square-number total distance pattern.
questions.prompt: Compare your total distance ratio column to the square-number pattern: 1, 4, 9, 16, and so on.
questions.requiredEvidence: Student should compare total distance ratios to square numbers and connect distance to time squared.

criteria: Identifies that total distance ratios are close to square numbers.
Connects the pattern to distance growing with time squared.
Mentions square numbers with little explanation.
Identifies the pattern but weakly connects it to the data.
Compares to the wrong pattern.
Claims total distance increases linearly.
Gives no useful comparison.

commonMisconceptions: The odd-number pattern applies to total distance ratios.
Distance increases by the same amount each interval.

feedback.partialCredit: Add how the square-number pattern shows falling distance depends on time squared.
feedback.noCredit: Use the total distance ratio column and compare it to 1, 4, 9, 16, and so on.

questions.objective: Identify measurement uncertainty in a digital experiment.
questions.prompt: Identify at least one source of error in the digital experiment and explain how it could affect the data.
questions.requiredEvidence: Student should name a plausible measurement or recording error and explain its effect.

criteria: Names a plausible source of error.
Explains how it could change measurements or ratios.
Names a plausible source of error with little explanation.
Explains an effect but the error source is vague.
Gives an unrelated error source.
Claims there could be no error without explanation.
Does not connect error to data.

commonMisconceptions: Digital simulations cannot have measurement or recording error.
Error only means the physics is wrong.

feedback.partialCredit: Explain how your named error would make a value too high, too low, or less precise.
feedback.noCredit: Choose an error related to reading, rounding, timing, scrubbing, or recording the chart.

questions.objective: Compare historical measurement uncertainty with modern tools.
questions.prompt: Explain why Galileo's water clocks, bells, or inclined planes could introduce more uncertainty than a modern digital simulation or video measurement.
questions.requiredEvidence: Student should compare limited precision and human timing uncertainty with modern repeatability or timing precision.

criteria: Mentions limited precision or human timing uncertainty in Galileo's tools.
Compares that uncertainty to modern digital timing or repeatability.
Says older tools were less accurate with limited explanation.
Gives a comparison but does not name timing, precision, or measurement uncertainty.
Does not connect the tools to uncertainty.
Gives an unrelated historical statement.
Does not compare old and modern measurement.

commonMisconceptions: Galileo's tools were exact because the pattern was correct.
Modern simulations always remove the need to think about precision.

feedback.partialCredit: Add a direct comparison between human timing or limited precision and modern repeatability.
feedback.noCredit: Focus on how timing and measurement tools affect uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Upload your completed Galileo data chart from the embedded lab above.
questions.requiredEvidence: The upload should show all time rows and all four calculated columns.

criteria: Upload is readable.
All time rows are visible.
All four calculated columns are filled in.
Upload is present but partially cut off.
One column or several rows are missing.
Values are visible but hard to read.
No upload.
Wrong file.
Evidence does not show the completed chart.

feedback.partialCredit: Upload a clearer image that shows the full completed chart.
feedback.noCredit: Return to the lab, complete the chart, and download or screenshot the evidence image.
